page: Microsoft Azure E48s_v6 is a memory-optimized virtual machine built on Microsoft Hyper-V virtualization. The instance provides 48 dedicated vCPUs derived from 24 physical cores of an Intel Xeon 8573C processor running up to 4.2 GHz. The x86_64 architecture incorporates 48 KB of L1d cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and a large 260 MB L3 cache pool. Architectural instruction extensions include AVX-512 (F, VNNI, BF16) and Intel AMX (tile and int8), accelerating vector calculations and localized machine learning workloads. Memory capacity totals 384.0 GB RAM, adhering to an 8.0 GB per-core allocation ratio. The server configuration includes no local instance storage and no dedicated hardware accelerators, depending on remote premium storage attachments for data persistence.

Benchmark evaluations position the E48s_v6 consistently in the upper tier across compute and memory-bandwidth metrics. Geekbench multi-core performance reaches 17,316.0 points, complemented by a Geekbench image processing score of 19,241.0, placing it in the top 10 percent of evaluated systems. Large-block uncached read bandwidth reaches 190.66 GB/sec in the top quartile, supporting high-throughput memory streaming. Synthetic integer and cryptographic throughput are reinforced by PassMark CPU tests showing 60,432.72 overall and 47,980.09 in encryption. For in-memory data management, the server achieved 63.01 million Redis SET operations per second and handled static web serving throughput at 78.62 GB/sec. Large model LLM prompt processing achieves 27.14 tokens/sec, aided by AMX matrix instructions, though PassMark composite memory scores fell into the lower quartile.

The 1:8 core-to-memory configuration delivers high resource density for workloads requiring vast address space without scaling unnecessary compute cores. Operational tradeoffs involve the absence of integrated local NVMe disks, requiring architectures to account for network-attached storage performance, and reliance on CPU-bound inference in the absence of GPUs. The E48s_v6 is suitable for large in-memory databases like Redis, enterprise ERP environments, high-capacity ETL pipelines, continuous integration compilation tasks, and quantized CPU-based machine learning inference.
